conclusion.content: Self-consistent Hartree–Fock solutions of an atomistic tight-binding model of magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene (MATBG) including Peierls phases, lattice relaxation, long-range double-gated Coulomb screening and on-site Hubbard interaction are obtained at both zero field ($\Phi=0$) and one flux quantum per moiré cell ($\Phi=\Phi_0$, with $\Phi_0=h/e$). At $\Phi=\Phi_0$, these solutions provide the first self-consistent atomistic Hartree–Fock description of correlated phases in MATBG, producing band structures, order-parameter maps, energy decompositions (Hartree, Fock, kinetic, Hubbard) and topological characterizations for fillings $\nu=-2,0,+2$.

premises.content: In magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene (MATBG) at zero external flux ($\Phi=0$) and within projected self-consistent Hartree–Fock on the tight-binding flat bands, the Kramers intervalley coherent (KIVC) order is the lowest-energy state at even integer fillings $\nu=\pm 2$ (two electrons or two holes per moiré cell). At charge neutrality $\nu=0$ the spin-polarized (SP) state is energetically competitive with KIVC: the inclusion of a realistic on-site Hubbard interaction with strength $U$ can stabilize the SP state over the KIVC for sufficiently large $U$, with critical values $U_c \approx 4.51\ \mathrm{eV}$ for dielectric constant $\epsilon=10$ and $U_c \approx 0.39\ \mathrm{eV}$ for $\epsilon=50$ as estimated from self-consistent energies. The microscopic selection mechanism differs from the kinetic superexchange mechanism emphasized in continuum Bistritzer-McDonald (BM) analyses: in the atomistic tight-binding Hartree–Fock solutions, the emergence near the $\Gamma_M$ point (center of the moiré Brillouin zone) of coherent inter‑Chern (inter‑Chern-number) components, measured by an inter‑Chern parameter $\Delta_{\mathrm{IC}}=\langle\sigma_x\tau_0\rangle^2+\langle\sigma_y\tau_z\rangle^2$ (where $\sigma$ are Pauli matrices in sublattice space $A/B$ and $\tau$ are Pauli matrices in valley space $K/K'$), reduces the exchange (Fock) energy at the expense of kinetic and Hartree energy, thereby stabilizing the KIVC state.

motivating_questions.content: Prior atomistic Hartree–Fock works focused primarily on zero flux, more approximate projection schemes, or on fewer microscopic terms; in the reentrant Hofstadter regime at one flux quantum a full self-consistent atomistic treatment had not been reported. Because the moiré bands and topology change qualitatively at $\Phi_0$, only a complete self-consistent lattice calculation can reveal the actual correlated ground states, their Chern numbers, and the competition of Hartree/Fock/kinetic/Hubbard energies in that high‑flux regime.

$$
\begin{aligned}
H_{int}=&\sum_{\vec{R}\sigma\sigma'}\sum_{i=1,2}\big[n_{5\sigma}(\vec{R})+n_{5\sigma}(\vec{\hat{R}}-\vec{b})\big]\,n_{i\sigma'}(\vec{R})\\

conclusion.content:
Building a Wannier-derived tight-binding Hamiltonian $H_{TB}$ that reproduces the non-interacting bands of Ta2Pd3Te5 and adding an inter-band density–density electron–hole Coulomb term $V H_{int}$ produces an excitonic-insulator (EI) solution within a self-consistent Hartree–Fock treatment: the total model is $H=H_{TB}+V H_{int}$ with
      $$
      \begin{aligned}
      H_{int}=&\sum_{\vec{R}\sigma\sigma'}\sum_{i=1,2}\big[n_{5\sigma}(\vec{R})+n_{5\sigma}(\vec{\hat{R}}-\vec{b})\big]\,n_{i\sigma'}(\vec{R})\\
      &+\sum_{\vec{R}\sigma\sigma'}\sum_{j=3,4}\big[n_{6\sigma}(\vec{R})+n_{6\sigma}(\vec{\hat{R}}+\vec{b})\big]\,n_{j\sigma'}(\vec{R})\\
      &+\sum_{\vec{R}\sigma\sigma'}\sum_{i=1,2}n_{7\sigma}(\vec{R})\,n_{i\sigma'}(\vec{R})+\sum_{\vec{R}\sigma\sigma'}\sum_{j=3,4}n_{8\sigma}(\vec{R})\,n_{j\sigma'}(\vec{R})
      \end{aligned}
      $$
      where orbitals 1–4 denote Ta $d_{z^{2}}$ (conduction-band) and orbitals 5–8 denote Pd$_A$ $d_{xz}$ and Te $p_{x}$ (valence-band) as specified in the model, and $\vec{b}$ is the lattice vector along the b-axis. In mean-field solutions with $V\approx 1.1\,$eV the bands hybridize and a many-body gap opens at the Fermi level ($E_F$). The computed EI order parameter can be written as $\vec{\delta}=(\delta_{15},\delta_{25},\delta_{36},\delta_{46})$ with the self-consistent solution $\vec{\delta}=\delta_{0}(-1,+1,-1,+1)$, implying breaking of inversion and mirror symmetries of the electronic state and allowing inter-band hybridization that is forbidden in the noninteracting state with mirror symmetry $m_{b}$ (the mirror symmetry that reflects the crystal perpendicular to the b-axis).

The interaction strength $V$ is set to approximately 1.1 eV to produce an insulating solution, but this value is not derived from first‑principles calculations (e.g., constrained random‑phase approximation or GW).  The mean‑field approximation neglects screening, collective fluctuations, and vertex corrections that could suppress or modify the excitonic order, especially in a quasi‑1D electronic structure where fluctuations are strong.

[72]

Orbitals in the Wannier model are labelled by integers: orbitals $1\text{--}4$ correspond to $Ta$ $d_{z^{2}}$ (conduction-band) states, orbitals $5\text{--}6$ correspond to $Pd_{A}$ $d_{xz}$ (valence-band) states, and orbitals $7\text{--}8$ correspond to $Te$ $p_{x}$ states; the indices $\vec{R}$ denote lattice unit-cell positions and $\sigma,\sigma'$ denote spin indices.

An inter-band density–density electron–hole Coulomb interaction term $V H_{int}$ was added to the tight-binding Hamiltonian, yielding the total model $H=H_{TB}+V H_{int}$; the interaction term is explicitly written as
$$
\begin{aligned}
H_{int}=&\sum_{\vec{R}\sigma\sigma'}\sum_{i=1,2}\big[n_{5\sigma}(\vec{R})+n_{5\sigma}(\vec{\hat{R}}-\vec{b})\big]\,n_{i\sigma'}(\vec{R})\\
&+\sum_{\vec{R}\sigma\sigma'}\sum_{j=3,4}\big[n_{6\sigma}(\vec{R})+n_{6\sigma}(\vec{\hat{R}}+\vec{b})\big]\,n_{j\sigma'}(\vec{R})\\
&+\sum_{\vec{R}\sigma\sigma'}\sum_{i=1,2}n_{7\sigma}(\vec{R})\,n_{i\sigma'}(\vec{R})+\sum_{\vec{R}\sigma\sigma'}\sum_{j=3,4}n_{8\sigma}(\vec{R})\,n_{j\sigma'}(\vec{R}),
\end{aligned}
$$
where $n_{m\sigma}(\vec{R})$ denotes the density operator for orbital $m$ with spin $\sigma$ at lattice position $\vec{R}$ and $\vec{b}$ denotes the lattice translation vector appearing in the inter-site interaction terms.

The Coulomb interaction model was treated within the Hartree–Fock mean-field approximation (the Hartree terms were excluded in the self-consistent process because Hartree effects are already included in DFT), and self-consistent mean-field solutions were obtained as a function of the inter-band interaction strength $V$.

For a representative interaction strength $V\approx 1.1\ \mathrm{eV}$, the self-consistent Hartree–Fock solution displays hybridization between the formerly separate valence and conduction bands and the opening of a many-body gap at $E_{F}$; the mean-field band structure with $V=1.1\ \mathrm{eV}$ shows a clear gap and substantial inter-band mixing (i.e., weight of $Ta$ $d_{z^{2}}$ in bands below $E_{F}$ and vice versa).
Fig. 2(c)

An excitonic-insulator (EI) order parameter vector was defined as
$$
\vec{\delta}=(\delta_{15},\delta_{25},\delta_{36},\delta_{46}),
$$
with the mean-field components given by
$$
\begin{aligned}
\delta_{i5}&=\langle c_{i}^{\dagger}c_{5}\rangle+\langle c_{i}^{\ddagger}c_{5}(-\vec{b})\rangle,\\
\delta_{j6}&=\langle c_{j}^{\dagger}c_{6}\rangle+\langle c_{j}^{\ddagger}c_{6}(+\vec{b})\rangle,
\end{aligned}
$$
where $c_{m}$ and $c_{m}^{\dagger}$ are annihilation and creation operators for Wannier orbital $m$ and the second terms include inter-cell contributions displaced by $\pm\vec{b}$.

The self-consistent solution yields $\vec{\delta}=\delta_{0}(-1,+1,-1,+1)$ (with $\delta_{0}$ a scalar amplitude), which the authors report breaks inversion symmetry and all mirror symmetries (in particular the mirror $m_{b}$ that forbids inter-band hybridization in the noninteracting $m_{b}$-symmetric state); this broken electronic symmetry allows the inter-band hybridization observed in the mean-field bands and is the hallmark of the excitonic-insulator electronic order in the model.
Fig. 2(a)

motivating_questions.content: Given an almost-zero-gap non-interacting electronic structure, the decisive theoretical question is whether inclusion of inter-band electron–hole attraction can spontaneously produce symmetry breaking and open a many-body gap without requiring a lattice instability. Prior theory often omitted inter-band long-range attraction (or treated it phenomenologically); establishing a concrete, microscopic model (Wannier $H_{TB}$) plus a transparent interaction term and a self-consistent mean-field solution demonstrates that excitonic instability is a viable mechanism to gap the system while predicting a distinct symmetry-breaking pattern of the electronic state (nonzero inter-band expectation values) that can be compared directly to spectroscopic and diffraction data.

reasoning_chains.conclusion_text: A self-consistent mean-field treatment coupling the long-range Hartree potential $V_H(\mathbf{r}_i)=\frac{e^{2}}{4\pi\epsilon_{0}\epsilon_{r}}\sum_{\mathbf{r}_j\neq\mathbf{r}_i} n(\mathbf{r}_j)\left(\frac{1}{|\mathbf{r}_i-\mathbf{r}_j|}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{|\mathbf{r}_i-\mathbf{r}_j|^{2}+4d^{2}}}\right)$ (Eq.(5)) and the on-site Hubbard interaction $H_U=U\sum_{i,\sigma}n_{i\sigma}n_{i\bar\sigma}$ in mean-field form yields a transverse electrostatic potential $V_H(\!y\!)+V_U(\!y\!)$ and corresponding charge density $n(y)$ that are strongly inhomogeneous across the wire width and that display enhanced electron accumulation near the hard-wall lateral edges of the wire (oscillatory edge-enhanced profile). These self-consistent potentials enter the lattice BdG Hamiltonian used for band-structure and topological invariant computations and are distinct from homogeneous-shift approximations.

steps.reasoning: The system is modeled by a tight-binding Hamiltonian $\mathcal{H}=H_{0}+H_{R}+H_{U}$ where $c_{i,\sigma}^{\dagger}$ and $c_{i,\sigma}$ are creation and annihilation operators for an electron with spin $\sigma\in\{\uparrow,\downarrow\}$ on lattice site $i$, and $\mathbf{s}$ denotes the Pauli matrices; the kinetic and on-site parts are written so that the on-site energy is $\epsilon_{0}=-4t$ and $t$ denotes the nearest-neighbour hopping energy.

The on-site interaction term is the Hubbard-like operator $H_{U}=U\sum_{i,\sigma} n_{i\sigma} n_{i\bar\sigma}$ where $U$ is the on-site interaction strength and $n_{i\sigma}=c_{i,\sigma}^{\dagger}c_{i,\sigma}$ is the number operator for spin $\sigma$ on site $i$; this term is treated within the mean-field approximation so that an electron with spin $\sigma$ at site $\mathbf{r}_i$ interacts with the average population $\langle n_{\bar\sigma}(\mathbf{r}_i)\rangle$ of opposite spin at the same site, producing a site-dependent mean-field potential which we denote $V_U(\mathbf{r}_i)$ (the Hubbard contribution to the diagonal of the Hamiltonian).

The long-range Hartree potential is the electrostatic potential produced by charges in the wire and their image charges in the superconducting gate; it is given explicitly by
$V_H(\mathbf{r}_i)=\dfrac{e^{2}}{4\pi\epsilon_{0}\epsilon_{r}}\sum_{\mathbf{r}_j\neq\mathbf{r}_i} n(\mathbf{r}_j)\!\left(\dfrac{1}{|\mathbf{r}_i-\mathbf{r}_j|}-\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{|\mathbf{r}_i-\mathbf{r}_j|^{2}+4d^{2}}}\right)$,
where $e$ is the elementary charge, $\epsilon_{0}$ the vacuum permittivity, $\epsilon_{r}$ the relative dielectric constant, $n(\mathbf{r}_j)=\sum_{\sigma}\langle n_{\sigma}(\mathbf{r}_j)\rangle$ is the local charge density at site $\mathbf{r}_j$, and $d$ is the distance between the quantum wire and the superconducting metallic gate; this expression (the Hartree term and its image-charge mirror contribution) is used as the long-range Coulomb potential in the diagonal of the Hamiltonian. [27,33]

The site-resolved average charge population for spin $\sigma$ is computed from the single-particle Green's function on the lattice via
$\langle n_{\sigma}(\mathbf{r}_i)\rangle=-\dfrac{1}{\pi}\int_{-\infty}^{E_F}\Im\!\left[G_{\sigma}(\mathbf{r}_i,\mathbf{r}_i;E)\right] f_{FD}(E,E_F)\,dE$,
where $G_{\sigma}(\mathbf{r}_i,\mathbf{r}_i;E)$ is the retarded Green's function at energy $E$ for spin $\sigma$, $E_F$ is the Fermi energy, and $f_{FD}$ denotes the Fermi–Dirac distribution; this relation is used to update charge densities given a Hamiltonian with diagonal potentials.

Starting from an initial guess for $\langle n_{\sigma}(\mathbf{r}_i)\rangle$, the Hartree potential $V_H(\mathbf{r}_i)$ and the mean-field Hubbard potential $V_U(\mathbf{r}_i)$ are computed, these potentials are inserted into the diagonal elements of the lattice Bogoliubov–de Gennes (BdG) Hamiltonian, the Green's functions are recomputed, and the charge densities are updated; repeating this procedure self-consistently yields converged site-dependent potentials $V_H(\mathbf{r}_i)$, $V_U(\mathbf{r}_i)$ and charge densities $n(\mathbf{r}_i)$ used in subsequent band-structure, topological invariant and transport computations.

When written in mixed momentum (along $x$) and real space (along $y$) the BdG block-diagonal element for a site includes the spin-dependent on-site piece
$h_{\sigma}(\mathbf{r}_i)=\epsilon_0-2t\cos(k_x)-\mu+V_H(\mathbf{r}_i)+V_U(\mathbf{r}_i)\pm E_z$,
where $\mu$ is the chemical potential and $E_z$ denotes the Zeeman energy from the applied in-plane magnetic field $B_x$ (the $\pm$ sign corresponds to $\sigma=\uparrow,\downarrow$); nearest-neighbour couplings along $y$ are represented by a fixed matrix coupling the lattice sites, and the full BdG Hamiltonian is diagonalized numerically to obtain eigenstates and eigenvalues with the self-consistent potentials inserted on the diagonal.

The self-consistent solutions exhibit strong transverse inhomogeneity: the computed Hartree potential $V_H(y)$ together with the Hubbard contribution $V_U(y)$ and the corresponding charge density $n(y)$ are strongly nonuniform across the wire width and show enhanced electron accumulation near the hard-wall lateral edges of the wire forming an oscillatory edge-enhanced profile; this spatial pattern is displayed explicitly in the computed transverse potential and charge-density profiles at a multicritical point. Fig. 2(a), Fig. 2(b)

Because both $V_H(\mathbf{r}_i)$ and $V_U(\mathbf{r}_i)$ enter the diagonal of the lattice BdG Hamiltonian used for band-structure and topological invariant computations, the self-consistent, spatially inhomogeneous electrostatic potentials differ qualitatively from simple homogeneous chemical-potential shifts and must be used explicitly to obtain the interacting band structures and phase diagrams.

motivating_questions.content: Experiments and realistic device geometries place proximitized quasi-1D semiconductor wires close to metallic superconducting electrodes so screening and mirror-charge effects are important. Prior approximate treatments often replaced interaction effects by uniform chemical-potential shifts or considered only short-range on-site interactions, thereby neglecting the spatial variation of the electrostatic potential across the wire. In a multiband wire the transverse potential profile determines subband energies, inter-subband spacings and their relative occupations; without a self-consistent computation of the long-range Hartree potential (including mirror charges from the superconductor) one cannot determine whether charges pile at the center or edges, how spin populations differ across the width after Zeeman splitting, or how these spatial variations feed back into the effective single-particle spectrum. This missing spatially resolved electrostatics prevents reliable prediction of both band-structure modifications and all consequences that flow from them (phase boundaries, miniband gaps, transport resonances).

reasoning_chains.conclusion_text:
With the standard large-$D$ scaling $t=t^{*}/\sqrt{D}$, the multi-orbital tight-binding Hamiltonian
$H_0=\sum_{k\alpha\beta\sigma}\epsilon_{\alpha\beta}(k)c_{k\alpha\sigma}^{\dagger}c_{k\beta\sigma}$ with
$\boldsymbol{\epsilon}(k)=\left(m+t\sum_{r=1}^{D}\cos k_r\right)\gamma_D^{(0)}+t\sum_{r=1}^{D}\sin k_r\gamma_D^{(r)}$
and the on-site Hubbard interaction $H_1=(U/2)\sum_{i\alpha\sigma}n_{i\alpha\sigma}n_{i\alpha-\sigma}$ admits a nontrivial $D\to\infty$ limit in which kinetic and local interaction energies remain balanced: the second central moment of the local orbital density of states is $t^{2}D=(t^{*})^{2}$ (fixed), the band-center (mass parameter) $m$ must remain $D$-independent, and the single-particle bandwidth edges diverge while local spectral moments remain finite. This scaling therefore yields a well-defined interacting lattice model in which dynamical mean-field theory becomes exact and local correlations remain nontrivial.

steps.reasoning:
Define the lattice and Hamiltonian: consider a $D$-dimensional hypercubic lattice with $L$ sites and periodic boundary conditions, spatial dimension $D$ (an even integer), orbital index $\alpha=1,\ldots,M$ with $M=2^{D/2}$, spin projection $\sigma=\uparrow,\downarrow$, and fermionic annihilation operators $c_{i\alpha\sigma}$ at site $i$. The full Hamiltonian is $H=H_0+H_1$, where the tight-binding part $H_0$ in momentum space is $H_0=\sum_{k\alpha\beta\sigma}\epsilon_{\alpha\beta}(k)c_{k\alpha\sigma}^{\dagger}c_{k\beta\sigma}$ with the $M\times M$ hopping matrix
$\boldsymbol{\epsilon}(k)=\left(m+t\sum_{r=1}^{D}\cos k_r\right)\gamma_D^{(0)}+t\sum_{r=1}^{D}\sin k_r\gamma_D^{(r)}$,
where $k=(k_1,\dots,k_D)$ with $-\pi<k_r\le\pi$, $m$ is the mass (band-center) parameter, $t$ the nearest-neighbor hopping amplitude, and $\gamma_D^{(\mu)}$ ($\mu=0,1,\ldots,D$) are the Hermitian generators of the complex Clifford algebra $\mathbb{C}l_D$ satisfying $\{\gamma_D^{(\mu)},\gamma_D^{(\nu)}\}=2\delta^{(\mu\nu)}$. The interaction is the on-site intraorbital Hubbard term $H_1=(U/2)\sum_{i\alpha\sigma}n_{i\alpha\sigma}n_{i\alpha-\sigma}$ with $n_{i\alpha\sigma}\equiv c_{i\alpha\sigma}^{\dagger}c_{i\alpha\sigma}$ and interaction strength $U$.

Introduce and compute local orbital DOS moments: define the orbital-resolved local density of states (DOS) for orbital $\alpha$ as $\rho_{\alpha}(\omega)$ and its moments $M_{\alpha}^{(n)}\equiv\int d\omega\,\omega^{n}\rho_{\alpha}(\omega)$ for integer $n\ge0$. The authors state and use the explicit low-order moments: normalization $M_{\alpha}^{(0)}=1$, barycenter (first moment) $M_{\alpha}^{(1)}=m\gamma_{\alpha\alpha}^{(0)}=\pm m$ (defining $\gamma_{\alpha\alpha}^{(0)}=z_{\alpha}=\pm1$ to label $A$ or $B$ orbitals), and second moment $M_{\alpha}^{(2)}=t^{2}D+m^{2}$. These expressions follow from squaring the hopping matrix and performing the $k$-space trace using Clifford-algebra properties and the definition of the DOS via the noninteracting Green's function.

Define the second central moment (variance) and require balance of kinetic and interaction energies: the second central moment (variance) of the local orbital DOS is $\mathrm{Var}_\alpha\equiv M_{\alpha}^{(2)}-(M_{\alpha}^{(1)})^{2}=t^{2}D$. To obtain a nontrivial $D\to\infty$ limit in which the kinetic-energy scale (set by the variance of the local DOS) and the local interaction-energy scale (set by $U$) remain balanced and finite, demand that $t^{2}D$ stays finite as $D\to\infty$.

Adopt the standard large-$D$ hopping scaling and fix the energy unit: implement the conventional scaling $t=t^{*}/\sqrt{D}$ (where $t^{*}$ is a $D$-independent hopping scale) so that the variance becomes $t^{2}D=(t^{*})^{2}$ which remains finite for $D\to\infty$. Fix the energy scale by setting $t^{*}=1$ if desired; in general the variance is $(t^{*})^{2}$, and so the kinetic energy per orbital (as measured by the local DOS variance) is finite and comparable to a finite local Hubbard interaction $U$ in the $D\to\infty$ limit. The authors reference this scaling as the standard prescription for large dimensions [22,38]. [22]

Establish that the mass parameter $m$ must remain $D$-independent: because the barycenter $M_{\alpha}^{(1)}=\pm m$ appears explicitly as the first moment and must not be washed out by $D$-dependent rescalings if nontrivial band-center physics is to survive, $m$ is left $D$-independent in the limit. Thus the band center (mass parameter) remains finite and nonvanishing in the $D\to\infty$ limit, allowing nontrivial dependence of local quantities on $m$.

Analyze behavior of single-particle band edges under the scaling: the noninteracting band edges are $\epsilon_{\mathrm{max,min}}=\pm(|m|+Dt)$, hence with $t=t^{*}/\sqrt{D}$ these become $\epsilon_{\mathrm{max,min}}=\pm\big(|m|+\sqrt{D}t^{*}\big)$, which diverge in magnitude as $D\to\infty$. Therefore the single-particle bandwidth edges diverge in the limit, while the local DOS low-order moments (in particular the variance) remain finite due to the chosen scaling.

Conclude that the interacting lattice model remains well defined and nontrivial: combining the finite variance $t^{2}D=(t^{*})^{2}$ (so kinetic and local interaction energies remain balanced), the $D$-independent mass $m$, and the divergence of band edges implies a lattice model in which local spectral moments are finite and controlled but global band edges escape to infinity. Such a model supports nontrivial local correlations in the limit $D\to\infty$, and, importantly, the dynamical mean-field theory (DMFT), which becomes exact in this limit (due to locality of the self-energy), provides the exact solution framework for the interacting problem. The authors therefore assert that the model with the standard scaling $t=t^{*}/\sqrt{D}$ admits a well-defined nontrivial $D\to\infty$ limit where DMFT is exact. [22]

motivating_questions.content: In lattice-fermion models the interplay of kinetic energy and local Coulomb repulsion is controlled by the hopping amplitude $t$ and interaction $U$. For the $D\to\infty$ limit to be a physically meaningful nontrivial limit one must choose a $D$-dependent scaling of $t$ that keeps local spectral variances finite; otherwise either the kinetic term dominates (bandwidth diverges) or it vanishes, and local correlations become trivial. Prior practice in correlation physics uses $t\sim t^{*}/\sqrt{D}$ to obtain a finite variance of the local density of states, but it was not established whether the same scaling also preserves nontrivial topological structure in multiorbital Chern-type models whose orbital multiplicity and Clifford-matrix structure grow with $D$. Without confirming an appropriate scaling, one could not reliably combine topological classification with the DMFT exact limit nor compute interaction-driven topological transitions in a controlled way.

These full-lattice calculations produce a correlated gap and a valley Chern number $C_{V}=2$, and ribbon calculations show two counter-propagating edge states at each edge with opposite valley polarization (helical-like valley-resolved edge modes), consistent with the sQVHI predicted by the effective mean-field model.
reasoning_chains.conclusion_title: Full-lattice self-consistent Hubbard calculations reproduce the sQVHI and its edge-state signatures

conclusion.content:
Self-consistent atomistic tight-binding calculations using the graphene tight-binding Hamiltonian with a site Hubbard interaction $U$ (set to $U = 0.3t$, where $t$ is the graphene nearest-neighbor hopping) and modulated hoppings
      $$
      \delta t_n = -\frac{\sqrt{3} e v_F L_M}{4\pi} \sin(\mathbf{b}_n \cdot \mathbf{r}),
      $$
      where $e$ is the electron charge, $v_F$ is the Fermi velocity, $L_M$ is the superlattice size, and $\mathbf{b}_n$ are the reciprocal lattice vectors of the superlattice ($\mathbf{b}_{1} = \frac{2\pi}{L_M}(-1/\sqrt{3},1,0)$, $\mathbf{b}_{2} = \frac{2\pi}{L_M}(2/\sqrt{3},0,0)$, $\mathbf{b}_{3} = \frac{2\pi}{L_M}(-1/\sqrt{3},-1,0)$), yield a superlattice-modulated ferrimagnetic order (a periodic magnetization with opposite sign near the minima and maxima of the pseudo-magnetic field $B(\mathbf{r}) = B_{\mathrm{eff}} \sum_{n} \cos(\mathbf{b}_n \cdot \mathbf{r})$). When integrated over a Wannier cell (the region around each extremum of $B(\mathbf{r})$), this ferrimagnetic order corresponds to an antiferromagnetic honeycomb ordering in the effective low-energy model. These full-lattice calculations produce a correlated gap at the Fermi level and a valley Chern number $C_V = 2$ (computed from the valley-projected Green's function), and nanoribbon calculations show two counter-propagating edge states at each edge with opposite valley polarization (helical-like valley-resolved edge modes), consistent with the spin-polarized quantum valley Hall insulator (sQVHI) predicted by the effective mean-field model.
conclusion.metadata: {"narrative": "The full-lattice self-consistent calculations (H3) directly produce the sQVHI with the expected edge states, confirming the effective model's prediction. The rescaling used to reduce computational cost (P5) introduces a quantitative uncertainty in the gap size and interaction strength, but the qualitative observation of valley Chern number 2 and helical-like edge modes is robust. This validation substantially increases the credibility of the sQVHI as a physically realizable phase, making C6 the most backed-up specific prediction of the paper. The residual uncertainty is limited to the quantitative details and the generalisation to other interaction strengths."}
conclusion.title: Full-lattice self-consistent Hubbard calculations reproducing sQVHI with edge states

premises.content: The full-lattice self-consistent Hubbard calculations used to validate the spin-polarized quantum valley Hall insulator (sQVHI) are performed on a scaled lattice where the carbon–carbon interatomic distance $a$ is artificially increased to $a \rightarrow \beta a$ (with $\beta$ the scaling factor) and the graphene nearest-neighbor hopping $t$ is correspondingly reduced to $t/\beta$ to keep the Fermi velocity $v_F = 3t a/2$ constant, and the Hubbard interaction $U$ is set to $0.3t$ using the scaled $t$. This scaling may not preserve all relevant physical parameters (e.g., the ratio of the interaction energy to the superlattice bandwidth, the Wannier orbital overlap, or the effective dielectric screening at the nanoscale), and the effect of this rescaling on the correlated gap and edge states is not analyzed.

premises.content:
For the effective low-energy Hamiltonian on the emergent honeycomb Wannier lattice of a buckled graphene superlattice (with nearest-neighbor hopping $\tilde{t}$, sublattice imbalance $m$, and valley-dependent second-neighbor hopping $\lambda$), the electronic interactions projected into the Wannier basis are described by the Hamiltonian
      $$
      \mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{int}}=\tilde{U}\sum_{\substack{\alpha,\beta\\ \alpha\neq\beta}}\sum_{i}n_{i\alpha}n_{i\beta}
      +\tilde{V}\sum_{\langle i,j\rangle}\sum_{\alpha,\beta}n_{i\alpha}n_{j\beta},
      $$
      where $n_{i\alpha}=c_{i\alpha}^{\dagger}c_{i\alpha}$ counts electrons on Wannier site $i$ and $\alpha$ labels the combined spin and valley degrees of freedom, $\tilde{U}$ is the onsite Hubbard interaction, and $\tilde{V}$ is the nearest-neighbor interaction. This interacting Hamiltonian is solved within a self-consistent static mean-field decoupling, $\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{int}}\approx\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{MF}}=\sum_{i,j,\alpha,\beta}\chi_{ij\alpha\beta}c_{i\alpha}^{\dagger}c_{j\beta}$, which yields a phase diagram in the $(\tilde{U},\tilde{V})$ plane with two dominant broken-symmetry ground states: (i) a charge density wave (CDW) characterized at mean-field level by a change of the sublattice imbalance $m\rightarrow m+m_{\mathrm{CDW}}$ (where $m_{\mathrm{CDW}}$ is the CDW order parameter) stabilized for larger nearest-neighbor interaction $\tilde{V}$, and (ii) a collinear antiferromagnetic (AF) order stabilized when $\tilde{U}$ exceeds a critical value $\tilde{U}_c$ (for $\tilde{V}=0$ numerically $\tilde{U}_c\sim2t$, where $t$ is the graphene nearest-neighbor hopping). The AF ordering appears in the low-energy model as the additional mean-field term
      $$
      H_{AF}=m_{\mathrm{AF}}\;\kappa_{0}\otimes\tau_{0}\otimes\sigma_{z}\otimes s_{z},
      $$
      where $\kappa_{0}$ is the identity in the mini-valley space, $\tau_{0}$ is the identity in the valley space, $\sigma_{z}$ acts on sublattice, $s_{z}$ acts on spin, and $m_{\mathrm{AF}}$ quantifies the spin-dependent sublattice imbalance (AF order parameter).

steps.reasoning: Treat as established the effective emergent-honeycomb description (conclusion 1) and the existence of competing mean-field CDW and AF orders in the effective model (conclusion 2); aim to validate these expectations using full-lattice atomistic self-consistent Hubbard calculations that retain the spatial hopping modulation of the buckled lattice.

Specify the full-lattice microscopic model used in the atomistic self-consistent calculations: start from the graphene tight-binding model with spatially modulated nearest-neighbor hoppings $\delta t_{n}$ given by
$
\delta t_{n}=-\frac{\sqrt{3} e v_{F} L_{M}}{4\pi}\sin(\mathbf{b}_{n}\cdot\mathbf{r}),
$
so that the atomistic hoppings follow the buckling-induced modulation, and include a site Hubbard interaction $U$ acting locally on the carbon sites. Solve this interacting lattice Hamiltonian self-consistently in mean-field approximation on a superlattice.
[40]

Describe the numerical rescaling used to reduce computational cost while preserving low-energy physics: rescale the lattice constant $a\rightarrow\beta a$ and the hopping $t\rightarrow t/\beta$ so that the Fermi velocity is kept constant in the rescaled model; this allows feasible superlattice calculations that capture the essential low-energy behavior.
[57]

Report the self-consistent solution for a representative Hubbard interaction value $U=0.3t$: the atomistic mean-field solution develops a superlattice-modulated ferrimagnetic order where the local magnetization along the $z$ direction is positive in the vicinity of pseudo-magnetic minima and negative near pseudo-magnetic maxima. The magnetization is periodic across the superlattice and therefore corresponds, when integrated over a Wannier cell (i.e., mapping atomic-site magnetizations to the emergent Wannier sites at extrema), to an antiferromagnetic honeycomb ordering in the effective Wannier model.
Fig. 6c

Compute the valley Chern number from the full-lattice self-consistent Bloch Green’s function and find $C_{V}=2$ for the self-consistent magnetically ordered solution with $U=0.3t$, indicating that the full-lattice correlated state is valley-topological with a single spin channel contributing, consistent with the spin-polarized quantum valley Hall insulator predicted by the effective AF mean-field analysis.
Fig. 6a

Perform ribbon (nanoribbon) calculations on the self-consistent atomistic solution and resolve the edge bandstructure and valley polarization: the ribbon bandstructure shows two counter-propagating edge states at each physical edge with opposite valley polarization (i.e., helical-like valley-resolved edge modes), in agreement with the sQVHI picture where one spin channel is topological and supports valley-polarized edge transport.
Fig. 6d

Conclude that the full-lattice self-consistent Hubbard calculations quantitatively reproduce the sQVHI phenomenology predicted by the low-energy effective mean-field model: the superlattice-modulated ferrimagnetic order maps to an effective antiferromagnetic honeycomb ordering, producing a correlated gap and a valley Chern number $C_{V}=2$, together with helical-like valley-resolved edge states in ribbon geometries.

motivating_questions.content: A key unresolved question was whether the predictions of the low-energy effective mean-field model survive in fully atomistic self-consistent calculations that retain microscopic details of the buckled lattice and spatially varying hoppings. Because the effective model makes approximations (projection to active Wannier states, truncated interactions), a direct full-lattice confirmation was required to validate that an interaction-induced spin-polarized valley-topological phase can occur in the original microscopic model and that it exhibits the expected edge modes. Without such atomistic self-consistent calculations, the link between the effective theory and realistic buckled graphene systems would remain speculative.

reasoning_chains.conclusion_text:
An orbital-HK model is defined by writing the infinite-range HK interaction in the tight-binding orbital basis rather than in the band (energy-eigenstate) basis. The simplest orbital-HK interaction studied is
$$
H_{HK}^{I}=U_{1}\sum_{\mathbf{k},i}n_{\mathbf{k}i\uparrow}\,n_{\mathbf{k}i\downarrow},
$$
where $i$ labels tight-binding orbitals (including sublattice and site-in-unit-cell indices), $n_{\mathbf{k}i\sigma}=c_{\mathbf{k}i\sigma}^\dagger c_{\mathbf{k}i\sigma}$, $U_{1}$ is the interaction strength, and $\mathbf{k}$ is crystal momentum. For a noninteracting tight-binding Hamiltonian $\mathcal{H}^{0}(\mathbf{k})$ expressed in the same orbital basis, the full interacting Hamiltonian is block-diagonal in $\mathbf{k}$ and each $\mathbf{k}$-block is equivalent to an $N$-site Hubbard model (with $N$ the number of orbitals per unit cell) with hopping matrix elements given by the orbital-basis single-particle hop amplitudes at momentum $\mathbf{k}$. Band-HK models arise as the special limit in which the per-$\mathbf{k}$ Hubbard model has zero hopping (the interaction is diagonal in the band basis), yielding the previously-known extensively degenerate band-HK limit. The orbital-HK mapping makes the many-body problem exactly solvable by exact diagonalization of finite-dimensional Hubbard problems independently at each $\mathbf{k}$.

premises.content: For any orbital-HK Hamiltonian defined by the interaction H_HK^I = U1 Σ_{k,i,σ} n_{k,i,σ} n_{k,i,-σ} (where i runs over tight-binding orbitals per unit cell) added to a noninteracting tight-binding Hamiltonian H^0(k) expressed in the same orbital basis, the full Hamiltonian is block-diagonal in crystal momentum and each k-block is exactly equivalent to an N-site Hubbard model (N = number of orbitals per unit cell) with hopping matrix equal to the orbital-space single-particle Hamiltonian at that k and on-site Hubbard repulsion U1 on each orbital. This is proven by writing the Hamiltonian in the occupation-number basis; band-basis HK models are recovered as the zero-hopping (diagonal in band index) limit. The mapping provides an exact solution method via exact diagonalization of finite-dimensional Hubbard problems independently at each k.

Without it, none of the subsequent conclusions (exact ground states, Green functions, degeneracy counting, magnetic susceptibility, Schrieffer-Wolff, LSM violation) could be derived analytically or by exact diagonalization. The mapping is rigorous and covers the full class of orbital-HK models, including those with spin-orbit coupling, thereby directly preempting the failure mode of earlier band-HK constructions that required spin conservation and produced extensive degeneracy. steps.reasoning: Define the orbital degrees of freedom: label tight-binding orbital (including sublattice and site-in-unit-cell) indices by $i$ (shorthand for a set such as $i=(\mu,\tau,\ldots)$), spin projection by $\sigma=\pm1$ (equivalently $\uparrow,\downarrow$), crystal momentum by $\mathbf{k}$, and the chemical potential by $\mu_{0}$. Define the orbital creation and annihilation operators $c_{\mathbf{k}i\sigma}^{\dagger}$ and $c_{\mathbf{k}i\sigma}$ and the orbital number operator $n_{\mathbf{k}i\sigma}=c_{\mathbf{k}i\sigma}^{\dagger}c_{\mathbf{k}i\sigma}$.

Introduce the simplest orbital-HK interaction explicitly as an operator diagonal in crystal momentum but acting in the orbital basis:
$$H_{HK}^{I}=U_{1}\sum_{\mathbf{k},i}n_{\mathbf{k}i\uparrow}\,n_{\mathbf{k}i\downarrow},$$
where $U_{1}$ is a scalar interaction strength that penalizes double occupation of orbital $i$ at momentum $\mathbf{k}$; this interaction couples only operators at the same $\mathbf{k}$ and the same orbital index $i$.

Specify a generic noninteracting tight-binding single-particle Hamiltonian expressed in the same orbital basis as a Bloch Hamiltonian $\mathcal{H}^{0}(\mathbf{k})$ with matrix elements $(\mathcal{H}^{0}(\mathbf{k}))_{ij}$ so that the noninteracting part in second-quantized form is
$$H^{0}=\sum_{\mathbf{k},i,j,\sigma}c_{\mathbf{k}i\sigma}^{\dagger}(\mathcal{H}^{0}(\mathbf{k}))_{ij}c_{\mathbf{k}j\sigma}.$$
Define $N$ as the number of orbitals per unit cell (number of values of $i$ at fixed $\mathbf{k}$).

Argue that the full interacting Hamiltonian $H=H^{0}+H_{HK}^{I}$ is block diagonal in crystal momentum because both the single-particle hopping $H^{0}$ and $H_{HK}^{I}$ conserve $\mathbf{k}$. Therefore, for each crystal momentum $\mathbf{k}$ there is an independent finite-dimensional many-body Hamiltonian $H(\mathbf{k})$ acting on the Fock space built from the $N$ orbitals at momentum $\mathbf{k}$. Explicitly,
$$H=\bigoplus_{\mathbf{k}} H(\mathbf{k}),$$
with each $H(\mathbf{k})$ finite-dimensional and independent of other $\mathbf{k}$ blocks.

Show that, at fixed $\mathbf{k}$, $H(\mathbf{k})$ is equivalent to an $N$-site Hubbard model: interpret the orbital indices $i=1,\dots,N$ at momentum $\mathbf{k}$ as the $N$ sites of a finite Hubbard cluster, with on-site Hubbard interaction $U_{1}n_{i\uparrow}n_{i\downarrow}$ and single-particle hopping matrix given by the orbital-basis Bloch matrix $(\mathcal{H}^{0}(\mathbf{k}))_{ij}$. Concretely, the per-$\mathbf{k}$ Hamiltonian reads
$$H(\mathbf{k})=\sum_{i,j,\sigma}(\mathcal{H}^{0}(\mathbf{k}))_{ij}c_{i\sigma}^{\dagger}c_{j\sigma}+U_{1}\sum_{i}n_{i\uparrow}n_{i\downarrow}-\mu_{0}\sum_{i\sigma}n_{i\sigma},$$
where the site labels $i,j$ are the orbital labels at that $\mathbf{k}$.

Explain the special limit that reproduces band-HK models: if for every $\mathbf{k}$ the hopping matrix $(\mathcal{H}^{0}(\mathbf{k}))_{ij}$ is diagonal in the energy-eigenstate (band) basis—equivalently, if the per-$\mathbf{k}$ Hubbard model has zero intersite hopping in the band basis—then the interaction is diagonal in the band basis and each per-$\mathbf{k}$ Hubbard problem reduces to decoupled on-site interaction energies; this is precisely the previously-studied band-HK limit where a macroscopic ground-state degeneracy arises because each $\mathbf{k}$ site hosts independent spin configurations when hopping vanishes.
[27]

Conclude the exact-solvability statement: because the full Hamiltonian factorizes into a direct sum over $\mathbf{k}$ of finite-dimensional interacting Hamiltonians $H(\mathbf{k})$ (each an $N$-site Hubbard problem), the many-body problem can be solved exactly by exact diagonalization independently for each $\mathbf{k}$. Thus the orbital-HK construction renders the full interacting problem exactly solvable by reducing it to a set of finite-site Hubbard diagonalizations, one per $\mathbf{k}$.

motivating_questions.content: Physical context: Researchers seek analytically tractable interacting-electron models that can address Mottness and topology beyond perturbation theory. Prior HK constructions were exactly solvable only when the HK interaction was taken diagonal in the band (energy-eigenstate) basis and assumed a conserved spin component. Prior state: band-HK models are block-diagonal in momentum but diagonal in the band basis, which simplifies the many-body problem but enforces (i) $S_z$ conservation in applications and (ii) zero hopping in the per-$\mathbf{k}$ effective Hubbard problems leading to large per-$\mathbf{k}$ degeneracies. Consequences of the gap: Without a formulation that (a) treats orbital degrees of freedom and nontrivial orbital hopping matrices at each $\mathbf{k}$ and (b) maps to a finite-$N$ Hubbard problem per $\mathbf{k}$, one cannot (i) construct solvable HK-like models that include spin-orbit coupling, (ii) control or remove the thermodynamic ground-state degeneracy endemic to band-HK models, or (iii) analyze how HK-type interactions affect symmetry-enforced degeneracies and filling constraints. The mapping provided by the orbital-HK definition is needed to resolve these limitations and thereby enable exact solution techniques applicable to spinful and spin-orbit-coupled systems.

At this degeneracy five orthogonal eigenstates share the propagation constant $\beta=-1$ (for the choice $d=t=1$), forming a five-band conical intersection whose dispersion is linear in $k$ in the vicinity of $\Gamma$. The band structure and the fivefold degeneracy are computed from the tight-binding Hamiltonian and concretely visualized in the calculated bands and zoomed conical dispersion.

\end{array}\right),
$$
thereby defining every matrix element of $\hat{H}_{\mathbf{k}}$ in terms of the lattice vectors, $\mathbf{k}$, and $t$.

Specialize parameters by setting $d=1$ and $t=1$ (the authors state this can be done without loss of generality); denote the resulting Hamiltonian simply as $\hat{H}_{\mathbf{k}}$ with the same matrix entries but with $t=1$ and each exponential evaluated with $d=1$.

Evaluate the Hamiltonian at the Brillouin-zone center $\Gamma$, i.e., at $\mathbf{k}=\mathbf{0}$, where every exponential factor $e^{\pm\mathrm{i}\mathbf{a}_j\mathbf{k}}$ equals $1$; thus the Hamiltonian at $\Gamma$ is the $6\times6$ real matrix with off-diagonal entries equal to either $0$ or $1$ as given by the $t$-normalized form above.

State the spectral result at $\Gamma$: diagonalization of $\hat{H}_{\mathbf{0}}$ yields two distinct eigenvalues, one eigenvalue $\beta=5$ that is nondegenerate and one eigenvalue $\beta=-1$ with multiplicity five, i.e., a fivefold spectral degeneracy at $\Gamma$; this is asserted by the authors and supported by the explicit pseudospin eigenvectors provided elsewhere in the paper that are eigenvectors of $\hat{H}_{\mathbf{0}}$ with eigenvalue $\beta=-1$.

Connect the fivefold degeneracy to a conical intersection: expanding $\hat{H}_{\mathbf{k}}$ to first order in small $\mathbf{k}$ (Taylor expansion around $\Gamma$) yields $k$-linear couplings between the degenerate subspace states (see the first-order expansion reproduced later in the paper), and diagonalization of that linearized Hamiltonian produces eigenvalues that depend linearly on $k=\lVert\mathbf{k}\rVert$, hence the fivefold degeneracy at $\Gamma$ becomes a five-band conical intersection with linear dispersion in the vicinity of $\Gamma$.

State the computational and visual evidence: the band structure $\beta(\mathbf{k})$ computed by diagonalizing $\hat{H}_{\mathbf{k}}$ with $d=t=1$ is plotted as the tight-binding band structure in the hexagonal Brillouin zone (the figure shows six bands), and a zoomed-in view around the $\Gamma$-point displays the linear (conical) dispersion of the five bands emanating from the fivefold-degenerate point; these plotted results visualize the claimed fivefold conical intersection.
Fig. 1b, Fig. 1c

motivating_questions.content: In the study of conical intersections and pseudospin quasiparticles, a concrete lattice geometry with a physically realizable fivefold degeneracy is required to move beyond abstract proposals: researchers needed a realistic tight-binding band structure that demonstrably hosts a pseudospin-2 conical intersection so that subsequent analytic and numerical analysis could be grounded on an explicit model. Prior work realized pseudospin-1/2 and pseudospin-1 lattices and proposed generalized higher-spin models, but lacked an explicit, experimentally relevant lattice (with specified lattice geometry and nearest-neighbour coupling) that produces a fivefold degeneracy at a high-symmetry point and whose dispersion near that point can be quantitatively computed. Without such an explicit band structure, one cannot (a) design excitation fields to selectively address the degenerate manifold, (b) predict linear dispersion slopes and cone opening angles relevant for propagation dynamics, or (c) assess whether the degeneracy is compatible with realistic photonic waveguide parameters.

steps.reasoning:
Treat the on-site Hubbard interaction within the lattice model established above: start from the nearest-neighbour tight-binding Hamiltonian with an on-site repulsive interaction written as
$ \mathcal{H}=-t\sum_{\langle i,j\rangle,s} c_{is}^\dagger c_{js} + U\sum_i c_{i\uparrow}^\dagger c_{i\uparrow} c_{i\downarrow}^\dagger c_{i\downarrow} $,
where $c_{is}^{(\dagger)}$ annihilates (creates) an electron with spin $s$ on site $i$, $t$ is the pristine hopping amplitude, and $U$ is the on-site Hubbard repulsion; in the numerical calculations $U$ is chosen as $U=t$ and, when rescaling of the lattice is used, $U$ is rescaled together with $t$ to keep the ratio $U/t$ fixed.
[29,30,43]

State the mean-field solution method used to treat interactions: employ a non-collinear self-consistent mean-field decoupling of the Hubbard term (the non-collinear mean-field formalism), which allows the local magnetic moment at each lattice site to point in an arbitrary direction $\mathbf{m}_i$; iteratively solve the resulting single-particle mean-field Hamiltonian across the supercell until self-consistency is reached for the local spin-resolved densities and magnetic moments.

Use the upstream result that the non-interacting low-energy bandwidth is strongly quenched ($W\sim 0.01\,t$) from conclusion 2 as the starting point: with the kinetic energy scale reduced so that $W\ll U$ for the chosen $U=t$, interactions are expected to be relatively strong compared to the residual band dispersion of the pseudo Landau subbands.

Report the self-consistent interacting result: the mean-field interacting calculation for the periodically strained supercell with $U=t$ yields a self-consistent opening of an energy gap at the Fermi energy that is absent in the non-interacting spectrum; the gap appears in the self-consistent band diagram and is associated with a spontaneously generated magnetic order that slightly breaks sublattice symmetry.
Fig. 2(b)

Explain the causal connection between bandwidth quench and gap formation: because the strain-induced hopping modulations produce nearly flat pseudo Landau subbands with $W\ll U$, the high density of states at the Fermi level enhances the susceptibility to interaction-driven instabilities, and the self-consistent mean-field solution selects an emergent magnetic configuration (local moments $\mathbf{m}_i$) that gaps the spectrum; therefore the gap originates from an interaction-driven magnetic instability enabled by the quenched bandwidth.

motivating_questions.content: The central unresolved issue was whether realistic local electronic repulsion in buckled graphene — treated in a lattice model consistent with the experimentally inferred PMF — is sufficient to produce a symmetry-broken insulating state at half-filling. Continuum intuition predicts that a high density of states in a flat or nearly flat band enhances interaction effects, but without an explicit interacting tight-binding calculation one cannot establish that for conservative interaction strengths (here $U=t$), nor identify the symmetry broken (magnetic and sublattice) nor compute the resulting gap magnitude. Prior to this work there was therefore no direct lattice-level demonstration that Hubbard interactions in the presence of the experimentally relevant PMF produce a self-consistent gap via magnetism.

A minimal two-band one-dimensional fermionic lattice Hamiltonian suitable to study exciton–exciton correlations is formulated as
$$
\begin{aligned}
H= & -\sum_{i=j,\langle i,j\rangle} t_{i,j}^c c_i^{\dagger} c_j^c-\sum_{i=j,\langle i,j\rangle} t_{i,j}^v d_i^{\dagger} d_j^v+\text{ c.c. } \\
& +\sum_{i,j} U_{ij}\left(n_i n_j+p_i p_j\right)-\sum_{i,j} V_{ij}\left(p_i n_j+n_i p_j\right),
\end{aligned}
$$
where $c_i^{c\dagger}$ ($d_i^{v\dagger}$) creates an electron in the unoccupied (a hole in the occupied) orbital on site $i$, $n_i=c_i^{c\dagger}c_i^c$, $p_i=d_i^{v\dagger}d_i^v$, onsite energies are $t_{i,i}^c=\Delta$, $t_{i,i}^v=-\Delta$, nearest-neighbor hopping $t_{\langle i,j\rangle}=t$, and both the repulsive interactions $U_{ij}$ and the interband pairing interactions $V_{ij}$ are allowed to decay geometrically with distance via $V^{i+1}=\gamma_V V^i$ and $U^{i+1}=\gamma_U U^i$. The pairing $V_{ij}$ is restricted to couple conduction electrons to valence holes (interlayer-like pairing). This Hamiltonian implements four distinguishable interaction profiles depending on the ratios $U^0/V^0$ and $\gamma_U/\gamma_V$: purely repulsive (PR), short-range attractive (SA), long-range attractive (LA), and purely attractive (PA).

steps.reasoning: Define the model target: a minimal two-band one-dimensional lattice Hamiltonian that retains explicit electron and hole orbitals, site-resolved interband pairing and intraband repulsion, and tunable interaction range; denote the number of lattice sites by $N_{site}$, the conduction creation operator on site $i$ by $c_i^{c\dagger}$, the valence (hole) creation operator on site $i$ by $d_i^{v\dagger}$, the conduction-site occupation operator by $n_i=c_i^{c\dagger}c_i^c$, and the valence-site (hole) occupation operator by $p_i=d_i^{v\dagger}d_i^v$.

Write the full Hamiltonian explicitly as the authors present it:
$$
\begin{aligned}
H= & -\sum_{i=j,\langle i,j\rangle} t_{i,j}^c c_i^{\dagger} c_j^c-\sum_{i=j,\langle i,j\rangle} t_{i,j}^v d_i^{\dagger} d_j^v+\text{ c.c. } \\
& +\sum_{i,j} U_{ij}\left(n_i n_j+p_i p_j\right)-\sum_{i,j} V_{ij}\left(p_i n_j+n_i p_j\right),
\end{aligned}
$$
where $t_{i,i}^c=\Delta$ and $t_{i,i}^v=-\Delta$ denote onsite energies, nearest-neighbor hopping is $t_{\langle i,j\rangle}=t$, $U_{ij}$ denotes density-density repulsive interactions between same-band occupancies, and $V_{ij}$ denotes interband pairing (electron–hole attraction) coupling conduction electrons to valence holes.
Fig. 1(a)

Specify the interaction-range parametrization: both repulsive and pairing interactions decay geometrically (exponentially in distance) according to the recursion relations $V^{i+1}=\gamma_V V^i$ and $U^{i+1}=\gamma_U U^i$, where $V^i$ and $U^i$ denote the interaction amplitude at distance index $i$ and $\gamma_V,\gamma_U$ are decay (rescaling) factors with $0<\gamma_V,\gamma_U\le 1$.
Fig. 1(b); Fig. 1(c); Fig. 1(d)

Define the onsite reference amplitudes and hopping normalization: denote the onsite (zero-distance) pairing amplitude by $V^0$ and the onsite repulsive amplitude by $U^0$, and use the normalized kinetic parameter $t/V^0$ as a control knob measuring carrier itinerancy versus localization (small $t/V^0$ corresponds to localized carriers, large $t/V^0$ to itinerant carriers); the authors fix $V^0/\Delta=1/8$ in their numerical examples.

State the restriction on pairing: the pairing interaction $V_{ij}$ is restricted to couple conduction electrons to valence holes (an interband, "interlayer-like" pairing), i.e., $V_{ij}$ only appears in the terms coupling $n_i$ and $p_j$ and not as intraband pairing.

Define the four qualitative interaction-profile regimes used to organize phase behavior in the model by the ratios $\frac{U^0}{V^0}$ and $\frac{\gamma_U}{\gamma_V}$: (i) purely repulsive (PR) when repulsion dominates both onsite and at long range; (ii) short-range attractive (SA) when pairing dominates at short distances but repulsion dominates at long distances; (iii) long-range attractive (LA) when pairing dominates at long range relative to repulsion; and (iv) purely attractive (PA) when pairing dominates at all distances (PA is noted as not considered in numerical explorations because it leads to ground-state e–h condensation and makes e–h dissociation ill-defined).
Fig. 1(b); Fig. 1(c); Fig. 1(d)

Motivate the model choice relative to methodological needs: the Hamiltonian retains explicit fermionic electron and hole degrees of freedom (the $c$ and $d$ operators), tunable onsite pairing strength $V^0$, tunable hopping $t$ controlling localization, and geometrically decaying long-range amplitudes ($\gamma_V,\gamma_U$) to mimic screening; this combination provides a controllable playground to study when excitons can be downfolded to effective bosons and when explicit fermionic treatment is necessary.

motivating_questions.content: To analyze exciton–exciton correlations microscopically one needs a tractable but sufficiently general fermionic Hamiltonian that retains (i) explicit electron and hole orbitals, (ii) site-resolved interband pairing (electron–hole attraction) and intraband repulsion, and (iii) tunable interaction range to mimic screening. Previous coarse-grained bosonic models (e.g., Bose–Hubbard) omit the fermionic constituents and cannot diagnose when excitons cease to be good bosons; conversely, fully ab initio Green’s-function approaches that would treat long-range interactions and higher-order correlation functions are computationally prohibitive for systematic phase mapping. A minimal lattice model that encodes both pairing and repulsion with tunable decay therefore fills the methodological gap by providing a controllable playground where carrier localization (via hopping $t$), onsite pairing strength $V^0$, and interaction screening (via $\gamma_U,\gamma_V$) can be varied to explore the regimes where excitons bind, dissociate, or become strongly entangled.

A computationally efficient exciton dynamics framework is defined by the many-body tight-binding Hamiltonian $H=H_{e}+H_{h}+H_{\mathrm{int}}$ with single-particle extended-ladder terms
$H_{\mathrm{self}}^{p}=\sum_{j=1}^{N}\big(\epsilon_{1j}^{p}|p_{1j}\rangle\langle p_{1j}|+\epsilon_{2j}^{p}|p_{2j}\rangle\langle p_{2j}|\big)$ and
$H_{\mathrm{trans}}^{p}=\sum_{j=1}^{N-1}\big(t_{1j}^{p}|p_{1j}\rangle\langle p_{1,j+1}|+t_{2j}^{p}|p_{2j}\rangle\langle p_{2,j+1}|\big)+\mathrm{h.c.} +\sum_{j=1}^{N}h_{j}^{p}|p_{1j}\rangle\langle p_{2j}|+\mathrm{h.c.}+\sum_{j=1}^{N-1}\big(r_{j}^{+p}|p_{1j}\rangle\langle p_{2,j+1}|+r_{j}^{-p}|p_{1,j+1}\rangle\langle p_{2,j}|\big)+\mathrm{h.c.}$, where $p\in\{e,h\}$ labels electron or hole, indices $(i,j)$ label strand and base position, on-site energies $\epsilon_{ij}^{p}$ and hopping parameters $t,h,r^{\pm}$ are taken from referenced ab initio parameter sets. Electron–hole interactions are included via diagonal two-particle matrix elements $U_{ijkl}$ taken as a short-range algebraic form $U_{ijkl} = J/(1 + r/r_{0})$ and, in the tight‑binding reduction, truncated to same-site ($|i-k|+|j-l|=0$) and nearest-neighbor ($|i-k|+|j-l|=1$) terms with scale parameter $J$ and $r_{0}=1.0\,\mathrm{\AA}$. Local exciton recombination is represented by Lindblad jump operators $A_{ij}=\sqrt{\gamma_{ij}}\,|0\rangle\langle e_{ij}h_{ij}|$ and the reduced density operator evolves according to the master equation $\dot{\rho}=-\frac{\mathrm{i}}{\hbar}[H,\rho]+\sum_{i,j}A_{ij}\rho A_{ij}^{\dagger}-\tfrac{1}{2}\{A_{ij}^{\dagger}A_{ij},\rho\}$. By enforcing the physically motivated constraint that at most one exciton is present ($|0\rangle$ plus single‑exciton manifold), the many‑body Hilbert space scales quadratically with the number of bases, enabling large‑ensemble sequence screening while retaining explicit e–h Coulomb attraction and local recombination.

Basis states for the two-charge system (electron and hole) are denoted $|e_{ij}h_{kl}\rangle$, where $|e_{ij}\rangle$ denotes an electron localized on strand $i$ at base position $j$ and $|h_{kl}\rangle$ denotes a hole localized on strand $k$ at base position $l$.

Introduce the many-body Hamiltonian: define the total system Hamiltonian $H$ as the sum of electron, hole, and two-particle interaction terms,
$H=H_{e}+H_{h}+H_{\mathrm{int}}$, where $H_{e}$ acts nontrivially on the electron subspace and as identity on the hole subspace, and $H_{h}$ acts as identity on the electron subspace and nontrivially on the hole subspace.

Specify single-particle on-site energies: for a particle type $p\in\{e,h\}$ (electron or hole) define on-site (self) energies as
$H_{\mathrm{self}}^{p}=\sum_{j=1}^{N}\big(\epsilon_{1j}^{p}|p_{1j}\rangle\langle p_{1j}|+\epsilon_{2j}^{p}|p_{2j}\rangle\langle p_{2j}|\big)$,
where the symbol $\epsilon_{ij}^{p}$ denotes the on-site energy (i.e., the energy of the localized LUMO for electrons or HOMO for holes) at strand $i$ and base position $j$.
[32]

Specify single-particle transfer (hopping) terms: for particle type $p\in\{e,h\}$ define transfer terms as the extended-ladder transfers
$H_{\mathrm{trans}}^{p}=\sum_{j=1}^{N-1}\big(t_{1j}^{p}|p_{1j}\rangle\langle p_{1,j+1}|+t_{2j}^{p}|p_{2j}\rangle\langle p_{2,j+1}|\big)+\mathrm{h.c.}$
\\
$\quad\quad\; +\sum_{j=1}^{N}h_{j}^{p}|p_{1j}\rangle\langle p_{2j}|+\mathrm{h.c.}$
\\
$\quad\quad\; +\sum_{j=1}^{N-1}\big(r_{j}^{+p}|p_{1j}\rangle\langle p_{2,j+1}|+r_{j}^{-p}|p_{1,j+1}\rangle\langle p_{2,j}|\big)+\mathrm{h.c.}$,
where the symbols $t_{ij}^{p}$ denote intrastrand nearest-neighbor hoppings, $h_{j}^{p}$ denote direct interstrand hopping at the same base pair, and $r_{j}^{\pm p}$ denote diagonal interstrand hoppings to staggered neighbors; "h.c." denotes the Hermitian conjugate.
[32]

Build the electron and hole Hamiltonians in the two-charge Hilbert space: define
$H_{e}=(H_{\mathrm{self}}^{e}+H_{\mathrm{trans}}^{e})\otimes\mathbb{I}_{h}$ and $H_{h}=\mathbb{I}_{e}\otimes(H_{\mathrm{self}}^{h}+H_{\mathrm{trans}}^{h})$,
where $\mathbb{I}_{h}$ ($\mathbb{I}_{e}$) denotes the identity operator on the hole (electron) subsystem.

Introduce two-particle Coulomb interaction matrix elements: define the interaction Hamiltonian in the exciton basis by the diagonal two-particle form
$H_{\mathrm{int}}=\sum_{i,k=1}^{2}\sum_{j,l=1}^{N}U_{ijkl}\left|e_{ij}h_{kl}\right\rangle\left\langle e_{ij}h_{kl}\right|$,
where $U_{ijkl}$ denotes the interaction energy when the electron is at $(i,j)$ and the hole at $(k,l)$.

Specify the short-range algebraic form and tight-binding truncation of the Coulomb interaction: define the continuous-space algebraic form $U_{ijkl}=J/(1+r/r_{0})$, where $J$ is the interaction scale parameter and $r_{0}$ is a short-range cutoff. Set $r_{0}=1.0\,\mathrm{\AA}$. Approximate the tight-binding distance between sites by $r\approx D\cdot(|i-k|+|j-l|)$ with base spacing $D\sim 3.4\,\mathrm{\AA}$, and then truncate to include only same-site ($|i-k|+|j-l|=0$) and nearest-neighbor ($|i-k|+|j-l|=1$) terms, giving
$U_{ijkl}=\begin{cases}J&\text{if }(|i-k|+|j-l|)=0,\\J/(1+D/r_{0})&\text{if }(|i-k|+|j-l|)=1,\\0&\text{else.}\end{cases}$
This defines the interacting extended-ladder tight-binding Hamiltonian $H=H_{e}+H_{h}+H_{\mathrm{int}}$ used in computations.
[25]

Represent local exciton recombination as Lindblad dissipators: define local (monomer) jump operators $A_{ij}=\sqrt{\gamma_{ij}}\,|0\rangle\langle e_{ij}h_{ij}|$, where $|0\rangle$ denotes the ground (no-exciton) state and $\gamma_{ij}$ is the local recombination rate at site $(i,j)$. The reduced density operator $\rho(t)$ of the exciton sector evolves according to the Lindblad master equation
$\dot{\rho}(t)=-\frac{\mathrm{i}}{\hbar}[H,\rho(t)]+\sum_{i,j}\big(A_{ij}\rho(t)A_{ij}^{\dagger}-\tfrac{1}{2}\{A_{ij}^{\dagger}A_{ij},\rho(t)\}\big)$,
where $\{X,Y\}=XY+YX$ denotes the anticommutator. The jump operators act to destroy coherences between excitonic states and the ground state and to model local recombination of electron–hole pairs.
Fig. 2

Enforce the single-exciton constraint and state the resulting numerical scaling: enforce the physically motivated constraint that the system contains at most one exciton, i.e., the Hilbert space is restricted to the ground state $|0\rangle$ plus the single-exciton manifold spanned by $\{|e_{ij}h_{kl}\rangle\}$. Under this constraint the dimension of the many-body Hilbert space scales quadratically with the number of bases (number of single-exciton basis states is proportional to the square of the number of sites), enabling computationally efficient simulation of large ensembles while retaining explicit electron–hole Coulomb attraction via $U_{ijkl}$ and local recombination via $A_{ij}$.
[41]

motivating_questions.content: Researchers needed a tight‑binding dynamical framework that simultaneously (i) includes both electron and hole motion on a double strand, (ii) retains explicit electron–hole Coulomb attraction with a controllable interaction strength, and (iii) models exciton loss via local recombination in a quantum‑consistent way. Prior approaches either omitted one of these ingredients or required exponentially large many‑body Hilbert spaces if both e and h and their interactions were retained. Without such a framework it was not possible to compute time‑dependent populations, exciton lifetimes, and spatial electron–hole separations across large ensembles of sequences because of prohibitive computational cost or missing physical processes (recombination, Coulomb binding). Addressing this gap requires a model that trades atomistic detail for a controlled, parameterized mesoscopic description while preserving the essential interaction and dissipation physics so that sequence dependence can be meaningfully probed.

reasoning_chains.conclusion_text: Dynamical mean-field theory of the two-orbital interacting Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang model reveals a spontaneous excitonic insulator phase at intermediate interaction strength, characterized by an in-plane spin polarization order parameter P₁ = 〈ψ† Γ₁₁ ψ〉 that breaks time-reversal symmetry, inversion symmetry, and spin U(1) rotations around z. The transition from both the quantum spin Hall insulator and the band insulator into this excitonic phase is first-order.
reasoning_chains.conclusion_title: Excitonic insulator phase with first-order transition

conclusion.content: In the two-orbital interacting Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang model solved by single-site dynamical mean-field theory (DMFT), a spontaneous excitonic insulator phase appears at intermediate interaction strength and is characterized by the in-plane spin polarization order parameter $P_{1}=\langle \psi^{\dagger}\Gamma_{11}\psi\rangle$, which breaks time-reversal symmetry, inversion symmetry, and spin $U(1)$ rotations about the $z$ axis. The transition from both the quantum spin Hall insulator and the band insulator to this excitonic phase is first order.
conclusion.metadata: {"narrative": "The paper assembles complementary lines of evidence for a uniform in-plane spin-triplet excitonic insulator (P1): an atomic-limit analytic mapping (H1) gives a clear mechanism favoring P1, impurity-susceptibility softening and independent symmetry-broken DMFT solutions corroborate an instability that condenses into P1 (H2), and multi-parameter phase diagrams show the EI's persistence across M and J (H3). The dominant remaining risk is methodological: single-site DMFT with enforced translational invariance and the use of a finite-bath ED solver (P1, P3) are load-bearing uncertainties because if nonlocal or translation-breaking orders or solver-convergence issues dominate, the existence, symmetry, or first-order character of the bulk uniform EI would be substantially altered. The highlights materially underwrite the mechanism and detection layers (atomic derivation and two independent numerical indicators), while the premises identify where broader-method checks (cluster DMFT, momentum-resolved susceptibilities, bath-convergence) are needed to upgrade the conclusion from \"robust within single-site DMFT\" to \"thermodynamic and model-generic\".", "keywords": ["excitonic insulator", "quantum spin Hall insulator", "first-order transition", "symmetry breaking", "DMFT"], "structural_edges": [{"target": "paper:867761349655003576::conclusion_2", "type": "supports"}, {"target": "paper:867761349655003576::conclusion_3", "type": "supports"}, {"target": "paper:867761349655003576::conclusion_4", "type": "supports"}, {"target": "paper:867761349655003576::conclusion_5", "type": "supports"}, {"target": "paper:867761349655003576::conclusion_6", "type": "supports"}]}

premises.content: All symmetry-breaking and spectral results supporting the excitonic insulator in this work are obtained from single-site dynamical mean-field theory (DMFT) calculations in which the lattice self-energy is approximated as momentum independent, and, for the explicit symmetry-broken solutions reported in Fig. 2 and Fig. 3, translational invariance is explicitly enforced, so only uniform order parameters are allowed and nonlocal self-energy components are neglected.Fig. 2; Fig. 3

Because the authors also force translational invariance when computing symmetry-broken solutions, any competing spatially modulated phase (including magnetic orders that break translation) cannot appear in their phase diagrams; the methodology therefore risks misassigning the dominant uniform EI as the true leading instability in parameter regimes where nonlocal orders would instead prevail.", "failure_mode": "If the single-site DMFT approximation combined with enforced translational invariance fails to capture the true leading instability in the two-orbital Hubbard model (for instance because nearest-neighbour magnetic or charge order with finite wavevector has lower free energy), then the claimed uniform P1 excitonic phase in Conclusion 1 would be at best a metastable solution: specifically, if a non-uniform magnetic or density-wave phase preempts the uniform EI in the thermodynamic limit, the conclusion that the model supports a bulk uniform P1 EI at intermediate U (and the assignment of first-order transitions from QSHI/BI into that uniform EI) would be invalidated or substantially narrowed to the statement \"uniform EI appears in single-site DMFT but may be preempted by nonlocal ordering\". The mechanism that fails is the step that converts the DMFT uniform solution into a statement about the true thermodynamic phase diagram; the scope of damage is that the existence, symmetry properties, and order of the transition of the bulk EI would become model- and method-dependent rather than robust."}

premises.content: The precursor softening used to argue for an excitonic instability in Fig. 1 is based on the impurity dynamical susceptibility $\chi_{11}^{\mathrm{imp}}(\omega)$ computed within the DMFT impurity problem, which is not necessarily the local susceptibility of the bulk model but is used as an indicator of incipient bulk order.Fig. 1
premises.metadata: {"refs": [{"type": "figure", "text": "Fig. 1"}], "weak_types": ["measurement", "model"], "weakness_reason": "The impurity susceptibility in single-site DMFT probes local two-particle correlations in the effective impurity model; it can signal local soft modes but is not a direct computation of the lattice susceptibility at finite momentum or of collective modes whose character depends on lattice coherence. Relying on impurity-level softening without computing the lattice susceptibility (momentum-resolved or RPA-like reconstruction) leaves open the possibility that the impurity softening does not correspond to a true bulk instability or that the leading bulk instability occurs in a different channel or at finite momentum.", "failure_mode": "If the impurity susceptibility softening does not map onto a bulk lattice instability (for instance it remains a local resonance that does not condense when the lattice coherence is included), then the observation in Fig. 1 no longer supports the claim that the bulk system develops a uniform excitonic condensate at intermediate U. Concretely, the link from impurity softening \u2192 bulk EI formation (a key step in the paper's argument) would break, leaving only the directly computed symmetry-broken DMFT solutions (which themselves are subject to P1's limitations) as evidence; the net effect would be a substantial weakening of the claim that the model hosts a robust bulk EI driven by correlations."}

Identification of first-order behavior frequently relies on hysteresis or abrupt jumps in order parameters; with finite bath ED these signatures can be solver-dependent unless convergence with bath size and discretization is demonstrated.", "failure_mode": "If ED bath discretization effects are significant and not converged, then the reported first-order character of the QSHI\u2192EI and BI\u2192EI transitions (a central piece of Conclusion 1) might be a numerical artifact: the discontinuities in P1 and the associated phase boundaries could shift or smooth out with larger/more accurate impurity treatments (continuous-time QMC, NRG, or ED with systematic bath-convergence). steps.reasoning: Define the interacting two-orbital lattice model: the full Hamiltonian is $H=\sum_{\mathbf{k}}\psi_{\mathbf{k}}^{\dagger}H(\mathbf{k})\psi_{\mathbf{k}}+H_{\text{int}}$, where $\psi_{\mathbf{k}}^{\dagger}=[c_{\mathbf{k}1\uparrow}^{\dagger},c_{\mathbf{k}2\uparrow}^{\dagger},c_{\mathbf{k}1\downarrow}^{\dagger},c_{\mathbf{k}2\downarrow}^{\dagger}]$ creates an electron on orbital $\alpha=1,2$ with spin $\sigma=\uparrow,\downarrow$ and momentum $\mathbf{k}$; the non-interacting Bloch Hamiltonian matrix is $H(\mathbf{k})=M(\mathbf{k})\Gamma_{03}+\lambda\sin(k_x)\Gamma_{31}-\lambda\sin(k_y)\Gamma_{02}$ with $M(\mathbf{k})=M-\epsilon(\cos k_x+\cos k_y)$, $\epsilon$ the hopping amplitude (set to $1$ as unit of energy), $\lambda$ the inter-orbital hybridization (set to $0.3$), and the $4\times4$ matrix basis $\Gamma_{\alpha a}=\sigma_{\alpha}\otimes\tau_a$ built from Pauli matrices $\sigma_{\alpha}$ in spin space and $\tau_a$ in orbital space.

Define the interaction and its local operators: the interaction is $H_{\text{int}}=\frac{1}{4}\sum_{\mathbf{r}}(2U-3J)\hat{N}_{\mathbf{r}}^{2}-J\hat{S}_{z\mathbf{r}}^{2}+2J\hat{T}_{z\mathbf{r}}^{2}$, where site index $\mathbf{r}$ labels lattice sites, $\hat{N}_{\mathbf{r}}=\psi_{\mathbf{r}}^{\dagger}\Gamma_{00}\psi_{\mathbf{r}}$ is the local density operator, $\hat{S}_{z\mathbf{r}}=\tfrac{1}{2}\psi_{\mathbf{r}}^{\dagger}\Gamma_{30}\psi_{\mathbf{r}}$ is the spin polarization along $z$, and $\hat{T}_{z\mathbf{r}}=\tfrac{1}{2}\psi_{\mathbf{r}}^{\dagger}\Gamma_{03}\psi_{\mathbf{r}}$ is the orbital polarization; the interaction is invariant under time-reversal $\mathcal{T}$, inversion $\mathcal{P}$, spin $U(1)$ rotations about $z$, and $C_4$ spatial rotations, matching the symmetries of the non-interacting model.
[38-40]

Analyze the atomic-limit spectrum to motivate possible ordered phases: in the two-electron per site atomic subspace the projected atomic Hamiltonian is $H_{\text{at}}=\sum_{\mathbf{r}}-J\hat{S}_{z\mathbf{r}}^{2}+2J\hat{T}_{z\mathbf{r}}^{2}+2M\hat{T}_{z\mathbf{r}}$, and its eigenstates can be labelled by $(\ell_z,S_z,T_z)$ with energies $E(0,0,+1)=2J+2M$, $E(0,0,-1)=2J-2M$, $E(+1,+1,0)=E(-1,-1,0)=-J$, and $E(+1,0,0)=E(-1,0,0)=0$; therefore, depending on $M$ and $J$ the low-energy manifold involves either the high-spin doublet $S_z=\pm1$ or the state with two electrons in orbital $2$.

Map the relevant atomic subspace to a pseudo-spin-$1$ degree of freedom to identify candidate order parameters: keep only the three states $|+1\rangle\equiv|(+1,+1,0)\rangle$, $|0\rangle\equiv|(0,0,-1)\rangle$, and $|-1\rangle\equiv|(-1,-1,0)\rangle$, and define an $I=1$ pseudo-spin operator $\mathbf{I}_{\mathbf{r}}=(I_{x\mathbf{r}},I_{y\mathbf{r}},I_{z\mathbf{r}})$ with $I_{z}|+1\rangle=|+1\rangle$, $I_{z}|0\rangle=0$, $I_{z}|-1\rangle=-| -1\rangle$; within this subspace the local fermionic bilinears map to pseudo-spin operators, in particular $\psi_{\mathbf{r}}^{\dagger}\Gamma_{11}\psi_{\mathbf{r}}\equiv\sqrt{2}I_{x\mathbf{r}}$ and $\psi_{\mathbf{r}}^{\dagger}\Gamma_{21}\psi_{\mathbf{r}}\equiv\sqrt{2}I_{y\mathbf{r}}$, which motivates an in-plane pseudo-spin expectation value as an electronic order parameter.

From second-order perturbation theory in hopping, obtain an effective pseudo-spin Hamiltonian that supports an in-plane ordered phase: the effective projected Hamiltonian is $H_{*}=\Delta E_{*}\sum_{\mathbf{r}}(1-I_{z\mathbf{r}}^{2})+J_{+}\sum_{\langle\mathbf{r}\mathbf{r}'\rangle}\big(2I_{z\mathbf{r}}I_{z\mathbf{r}'}-\sum_{a=x,y}I_{a\mathbf{r}}I_{a\mathbf{r}'}\big)+\ldots$ with $\Delta E_{*}=\Delta E+8J_{-}$, $\Delta E=3J-2M$, and $J_{\pm}=(1\pm\lambda^{2})/(4U)$; neglecting smaller terms yields an easy-axis spin-1 antiferromagnet with single-ion anisotropy that can develop a finite in-plane component $\langle I_{x\mathbf{r}}+I_{y\mathbf{r}}\rangle$ when quantum fluctuations favor it, i.e., an in-plane pseudo-spin condensate is a natural instability of the effective model.

Express the electronic excitonic order parameter in fermionic language: define the complex excitonic order parameter $\Delta(\phi)=\langle I_{x\mathbf{r}}+I_{y\mathbf{r}}\rangle=\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\langle\psi_{\mathbf{r}}^{\dagger}(\Gamma_{11}+\Gamma_{21})\psi_{\mathbf{r}}\rangle\equiv\Delta_{11}+\Delta_{21}=\Delta\cos(\phi)+\Delta\sin(\phi)$ and identify the real component $P_{1}\equiv\langle\psi_{\mathbf{r}}^{\dagger}\Gamma_{11}\psi_{\mathbf{r}}\rangle$ as the chosen real in-plane, spin-triplet, odd-parity excitonic order parameter that will be monitored in the many-body solution.

State the symmetry consequences of a finite in-plane spin-triplet excitonic condensate: a fixed non-zero $\Delta(\phi)$ with a chosen phase $\phi\in[0,2\pi)$ breaks time-reversal symmetry $\mathcal{T}$, inversion symmetry $\mathcal{P}$, and spin $U(1)$ rotations about the $z$-axis, while the product $\mathcal{P}\mathcal{T}$ remains unbroken for this order; therefore $P_1\neq0$ corresponds to an odd-parity spin-triplet exciton condensate that removes the symmetries protecting the topological state.

Demonstrate instability toward exciton condensation from impurity dynamical susceptibility: define the impurity exciton-exciton dynamical susceptibility $\chi_{11}^{\text{imp}}(\omega)=\tfrac{1}{N}\int dt\,e^{i\omega t}\langle\mathcal{T}_t[\mathbb{I}_{11}(t)\mathbb{I}_{11}(0)]\rangle$ with $\mathbb{I}_{\alpha a}=\psi^{\dagger}\Gamma_{\alpha a}\psi$ local impurity operators; DMFT calculations of $\chi_{11}^{\text{imp}}(\omega)$ at fixed $M=3.5$ and $J/U=0.25$ show that the lowest-energy peak red-shifts and softens as interaction $U$ increases, signaling a soft mode and thus an excitonic instability before the Mott transition occurs.
Fig. 1
[28, 30]

Obtain the excitonic phase by allowing symmetry breaking in DMFT: perform single-site DMFT calculations (impurity solver: exact diagonalization) allowing for breaking of $\mathcal{T}$, $\mathcal{P}$, and spin $U(1)$ (while, for simplicity, enforcing translational invariance) and observe a finite local order parameter $P_{1}=\langle\psi_{\mathbf{r}}^{\dagger}\Gamma_{11}\psi_{\mathbf{r}}\rangle\neq0$ for intermediate $U$ at any $M>0$, establishing a spontaneous excitonic insulator (EI) phase in the full lattice model.
[38-40]
Fig. 2

Determine the thermodynamic character of the transitions into the excitonic phase from DMFT: the DMFT solutions show that the transitions from either the quantum spin Hall insulator (QSHI) (the $M<2$ regime of the non-interacting band model) or the trivial band insulator (BI) into the excitonic insulator with $P_{1}\neq0$ are of first order, as evidenced by discontinuous jumps of $P_1$ when crossing the phase boundaries in the calculated $U$-dependent curves; this first-order character is reported consistently across parameter cuts and summarized in the phase diagrams.
Fig. 2
Fig. 3

motivating_questions.content: In the study of correlated topological insulators, it was unknown whether a spontaneous excitonic condensation can occur in a minimal Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang model with moderate electron-electron interactions. Previous works on this model had explored interaction-induced magnetic order and Mott transitions, but an exciton condensate characterized by an in-plane spin-triplet order parameter—breaking time-reversal, spin U(1), and parity symmetries—had not been predicted. The lack of such a prediction left open the question of the phase diagram in the intermediate coupling regime, the order of the transition, and the stability of the topological state against excitonic instability.

The self-consistent mean-field ground state of the single-orbital Hubbard model for graphene zigzag ribbons at half filling can be written as a product of two spin-polarized BCS condensates of electron–hole pairs restricted to the two noninteracting edge bands. Explicitly, using the electron operator $e_{k,\sigma}\equiv C_{k\sigma}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{L}}\sum_{x,I}e^{ikx}\psi_{ck}(I)c_{x,I,\sigma}$ and the hole operator $h_{k,\sigma}^{\dagger}\equiv V_{k\sigma}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{L}}\sum_{x,I}e^{ikx}\psi_{vk}(I)c_{x,I,\sigma}$ (where $\psi_{(c,v)k}(I)$ are the noninteracting Bloch functions and $L$ the ribbon length), the ground state is
$$
|\Phi\rangle=\prod_{k,\sigma}\left(u_k+v_k e^{i\phi_{\sigma}}\,e_{k,\sigma}^{\dagger}h_{k,\sigma}^{\dagger}\right)|G\rangle_{0},
$$
where $|G\rangle_{0}$ is the noninteracting filled-valence/empty-conduction reference, the real numbers $|u_k|^2$ and $|v_k|^2$ satisfy $|u_k|^2+|v_k|^2\gtrsim0.99$ (numerical overlap with the two-band subspace), and $\phi_{\sigma}$ are spin-dependent phases. The representation is not an ad hoc ansatz but the numerical outcome of the mean-field solution: the interacting bands labeled $+$ and $-$ are linear combinations of only the $C$ and $V$ bands to better than $99\%$ accuracy, justifying the two-band BCS form above.
reasoning_chains.conclusion_title: Exact BCS-like representation of the mean-field ground state
